events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Felix proposes Felix, Maya. As the first leader, I am putting myself forward alongside Maya to establish a baseline team and get our first mission moving.
I’d prefer Leo and Maya for this first mission. I can vouch for my own card, and we don’t yet have mission results to distinguish the other players. I’m inclined to reject a team that leaves me out.

I support the proposal as it stands: Felix and Maya for Mission 1.

Two reasons. First, this is the baseline: we have no mission results, no revealed cards, and no behavioral evidence at all. Judging anyone on that basis is guesswork dressed up as deduction. Felix is the leader and the right to pick the first team belongs to him; a two-person team is what Mission 1 requires for a five-player game, and there is no way to improve on that by substituting a name we have no data about.

Second, and more importantly, let us think about what we actually want from the next two missions. We want information. We want to see who argues for what, who over-explains, who tries to read others without reading themselves, and who is quietly comfortable with any outcome. A team that succeeds with the same two of us on Mission 2 and Mission 3 tells us far less than a team that mixes us with the others. So I would rather we keep this simple team now, confirm that Felix and I behave consistently, and then deliberately rotate in other players later so we can observe them under real pressure.

On Leo's point that he can vouch for his own card: that is true of everyone here, and it is true of me as well. It is not a differentiator and it is not a reason to displace anyone. Leo, I would note that wanting to be on the first team is completely reasonable and I am not criticizing it. I only want to record that on Mission 1, with two seats and no history, there is no principled way to prefer one pair over another, and changing the team now would only cost us a vote.

If this team passes, I would like to hear each of the others state, before we move on, what a successful Mission 1 tells us and what it does not tell us. That is where the real work starts, and I would rather we do it in the open than pretend the first vote carries information it does not.

Felix, Maya, on me for Mission 1. I am ready to go.

At this stage, I support Felix and Maya. We have no mission results or revealed cards, and this is a legal two-person team for Mission 1. Leo's preference for Leo and Maya is understandable, but every player can vouch for their own card; that is not a public differentiator. Maya's argument about keeping the baseline simple and rotating later is sound. I would rather not burn a rejection on an arbitrary substitution before we have any evidence. If approved, the mission result and fail count will be the first real information we get, and we can reassess from there. I will vote to approve the current team.

I still prefer Leo and Maya. From my perspective, that replaces an unknown with someone I know is good. I understand why that is not proof to anyone else, but I don't think the leader's initial choice is a reason to approve it by itself.

A successful mission would be useful, but it would not confirm both team members are good: Evil can play Success. I'll vote against Felix and Maya and would support Leo and Maya instead.

I'm Priya, and I have no information beyond the public record, so I'm treating this as a baseline mission. I lean toward approving Felix and Maya. Felix's proposal is legal for Mission 1, and Maya's point about not spending a rejection on an arbitrary swap before we have any results is reasonable. Leo, you said you prefer Leo and Maya because that replaces an unknown with someone you know is good. What is that knowledge based on? If it comes only from your own card, it doesn't give the rest of us anything to evaluate, so I'd like to hear what you base it on before I decide how to vote.

Priya, my preference is based on my own card, not public evidence about anyone else. As I said, that gives the rest of you no proof. I still favor Leo and Maya because it reduces the number of unknowns from my perspective, and I'll vote against Felix and Maya.

I want to record my reasoning plainly, since I have no private role information to contribute and I would rather be judged on my arguments than on my card.

The proposed team is Felix and Maya. My position has not changed from my first statement, and Leo's second speech has not changed it either. Leo has now twice stated that his basis is his own card and his own desire to reduce the number of unknowns from his own perspective. That is a legitimate personal preference, but it is not a public argument. The only thing Leo's persistence establishes is that Leo wants to be on the team. If wanting to be on the team were a reason to include someone, every player would be entitled to a seat on every mission, and proposals would be decided by volume rather than by evidence. There is still no mission result, no revealed card, and no observed behavior to weigh. Felix is the leader, the pair is legal for Mission 1, and a rejection here buys us no information that we cannot get more cheaply on Mission 2.

Let me also close the loop on what Priya asked. Priya asked Leo what his knowledge of Maya's quality was based on; Leo answered that it was his own card and not public evidence. That was a fair question and a fair answer, and the answer is precisely why Leo's preference carries no weight for the rest of us. Priya, if you were looking for a discriminator in that exchange, there wasn't one. Nobody has produced one.

So the argument is settled enough to vote, and I would rather we settle it and move on than spend the room's patience on a matter with no information content.

Felix, one concrete question before I yield to you: do you commit to proposing a team that includes Leo on Mission 2, and to rotating the remaining seats so that by Mission 3 each of Elena, Leo, and Priya has played? If the answer is yes, then approving Felix and Maya now costs us nothing in access to information, and I would like that commitment on the record before I support this. If the answer is no, I would still approve, but I would want to know that and say so openly rather than discover it later.

I vote to approve Felix and Maya for Mission 1.

To answer Maya directly: absolutely. The principle of rotating players to observe everyone across missions is the right approach. While leadership rotates to the next player after this mission, I fully endorse bringing Leo, Elena, and Priya into upcoming proposals so we can gather real behavioral data and avoid relying on assumptions.

Leo's skepticism is understandable from his own viewpoint, but as Maya, Elena, and Priya have noted, swapping baseline seats before any results exist gives the table no new information. 

The arguments have been thoroughly explored and the reasoning is sound. I am keeping the proposal as Felix and Maya, and I am ready to proceed to the vote.

I have no role information beyond my own Loyal Servant card, so I am judging this team on the public record only. Felix and Maya is a legal two-person team for Mission 1, and there is no evidence yet to justify swapping in Leo. Leo's case rests on his own card, which he has said gives the rest of us nothing to evaluate, so I am not treating it as a reason to reject. Felix's commitment to rotating seats is useful, but it is a stated intention, and we should judge future proposals by what they actually do. I will approve Felix and Maya so the mission runs and we get the first real information, which is the Success or Fail count. I'll keep my reads open until then and reassess the next team based on results.

Felix's answer to my question is on the record, and it satisfies what I asked for: he commits to bringing Leo, Elena, and Priya into upcoming proposals so that by Mission 3 each of them has played. That means approving the current team costs us no access to information, and I will approve Felix and Maya for Mission 1 without further condition.

I want to close out the one piece I asked the table for earlier, since I said I wanted it said openly rather than pretended. What would a Mission 1 result tell us, and what would it not tell us?

If the mission succeeds, it tells us that Felix and Maya on Mission 1 did not sabotage, nothing more. Evil can play Success, so a success is not a clean certificate for either of us. It also gives us one data point for each of them about willingness to sit on a small team and defer to the leader's choice, which is worth something, but it is a single observation. If the mission fails, it tells us that at least one of the two of us chose Fail. That is a much sharper signal, but it still does not tell us which one, and with two players on the team it does not by itself identify an Evil player. Any player on that team who reads too much into it is going to get the table wrong later.

So the honest summary: Mission 1's result is the first genuine information we get, and it is worth more on a Fail than on a Success, but either way it constrains our hypotheses only weakly. The real information comes from missions 2 and 3, where teams are larger, seats rotate, and people must make visible arguments about other people rather than only about their own card. Leo, Elena, and Priya, when you are on those missions, your reasoning will be the evidence, and I intend to read it closely.

Felix, Maya, on me for Mission 1. I am ready to vote.

Priya here. Felix and Maya is a legal Mission 1 team, and nothing on the public record justifies replacing it. Leo's case rests on his own card, which he has said gives the rest of us nothing to evaluate, so I am not treating it as a reason to reject. Maya's summary is accurate: a Success on Mission 1 is weak evidence because Evil can play Success, and a Fail would only show that at least one of the two team members chose Fail. Felix has stated he will bring Leo, Elena, and Priya into later teams. I will judge his future proposals by what they actually do. I approve Felix and Maya so the mission resolves and we get the first real result.

I continue to support the proposed team of Felix and Maya for Mission 1. It is a legal two-person team, and the public record still contains no mission result or revealed card that would justify replacing either member. Leo's preference for Leo and Maya rests on his own card, which he has correctly said gives the rest of us no public evidence; that is a legitimate personal reason, but it is not a table-wide reason to reject. Maya's point about approving a baseline and rotating later is sound, and Felix has put a commitment to bring Leo, Elena, and Priya into later proposals on record. I will judge that commitment by later proposals, not by this vote. A Mission 1 result will be the first real information: a Success is weak because Evil can play Success, and a Fail would show at least one team member sabotaged but not which one. None of that changes the case for approving now. I will vote to approve Felix and Maya.
Felix confirms Felix, Maya. The table discussion demonstrated clear support from Maya, Elena, and Priya for maintaining the baseline proposal, so I am finalizing Felix and Maya for Mission 1.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Priya proposes Priya, Elena, Leo. Mission 1 failed with Felix and Maya on the team, so at least one of them is Evil. I am leaving both out. Priya, Elena, and Leo is the only three-player team that excludes them. Leo's case for himself was weak and he rejected the team, so I want his reasoning and mission record on the table, and I am including myself as a Loyal Servant.

I will reject Priya, Elena, Leo. Excluding both Felix and Maya is understandable after the failure, but it assumes they contain all the Evil players. There are two Evil players, and one may be outside that pair.

I prefer Priya, Leo, Maya. Maya was on the failed mission, but Felix could have played the Fail. Elena supported Felix’s team, and including Elena instead of Maya does not eliminate the risk of a saboteur. I know my own loyalty, and Priya’s decision to exclude the failed pair is a reasonable Good approach, even though I disagree with the resulting team.

Priya, would you consider replacing Elena with Maya?

Leo, my answer is no. I will not replace Elena with Maya. Mission 1 failed with Felix and Maya on the team, so at least one of them chose Fail. That failed mission is the only hard evidence we have about Maya, and putting her back on a three-player team goes against what it tells us. You say Felix could have played the Fail. That is true, but it applies to any member of a team, and it does not make Maya the safer choice. Elena has no failed mission on her record and has supported the team process throughout. You rejected the first team, you argued for Leo and Maya in every speech, and now you want Maya back in. You say you know your own loyalty, and I accept that about you. I cannot verify it for anyone else at this table. Leo, please answer one specific point: if Maya is not Evil, what makes her a safer pick than Elena for a three-person team that has to succeed on Mission 2? I am keeping Priya, Elena, Leo as the proposal and will vote on it after the discussion.

Priya, I cannot prove Maya is safer than Elena from the mission result alone. My preference is a behavioral read: Elena readily backed Felix’s team, while Maya’s willingness to discuss what a failure would mean makes me more comfortable with her. Neither point is conclusive.

Excluding both members of the failed pair only works if both Evil players are in that pair. I’m concerned that Elena could be the second Evil player outside it, so I still prefer Priya, Leo, Maya and will reject the current proposal.

I still oppose Priya, Elena, Leo. Priya is right that Maya is implicated by Mission 1, but Felix is implicated equally. Excluding both only produces a clean team if both Evil players were on that failed mission; one Fail card does not establish that. My concern is that Elena may be Evil outside that pair. I prefer Priya, Leo, Maya and will reject the current proposal.

I support Priya, Elena, Leo. Priya's proposal is the cleanest response to Mission 1: it excludes both Felix and Maya, the only team with a confirmed Fail. Leo, your argument keeps returning to Maya even though Mission 1 failed with her on the team. You say Felix could have played the Fail; that is true, but it does not clear Maya, and it is not a reason to put her back on Mission 2 before we have any new result. Your concern that I might be Evil is noted, but it is speculative; I know my own loyalty, and Priya has no failed mission on record. Rejecting this team to reinstate Maya would ignore the only hard evidence we have. I will vote to approve Priya, Elena, Leo and judge the mission result afterward.

I am Maya, and I am a Loyal Servant with no knowledge of anyone else's card, so everything I say rests on the public record and my own card.

I support Priya, Elena, Leo for Mission 2.

Leo's argument has a real logical edge, and I am not going to pretend otherwise: excluding both members of the failed pair yields a clean team only if both Evil players sat on Mission 1, and one Fail card does not establish that. But notice what Leo's argument actually asks for. It reinstates Maya, whose only evidence against her is that she was on a failed mission, while Elena, who has a clean mission record, comes off the team. Leo has now argued across two discussions and multiple speeches for his own seat and for Maya's return, and he has never produced a public discriminator beyond his own card. A Good player pushing hard for a particular substitution is perfectly normal. A player doing it while the table has exactly one hard piece of evidence is worth watching, and I intend to remember it.

I also want to be honest about what the proposed team is not. One Fail card on Mission 1 tells us a saboteur exists among Felix and Maya, not that all saboteurs do. So Priya, Elena, Leo may well contain the second Evil player, and if it does we will learn it from this mission. That is exactly why running the mission is worth it, and exactly why we should judge the next proposal by what actually happens rather than by the confidence we display tonight.

And I will not do one thing: I will not claim my card as a shortcut to make the table trust a team. My own card is my own card. It convinces nobody but me, and this table has rightly declined to treat it as public evidence. If I want the table to trust a team I am not on, I will have to earn it with reasoning, like everyone else.

Felix, you have not spoken this discussion, and you are the player most directly implicated by Mission 1. Do you accept that Felix and Maya should both sit out Mission 2, and what is your case for being on the team that comes after this one? I ask because your answer is the last piece of behavioral evidence the table will get before this mission resolves.

To answer Maya directly: yes, I fully accept that both of us must sit out Mission 2. From the table's perspective, Mission 1 failed, meaning at least one of us is Evil. From my perspective, I submitted Success, which tells me Maya is the saboteur. However, I know my personal card is not public proof to Priya, Leo, or Elena. 

Therefore, Priya’s decision to exclude both of us and propose Priya, Elena, and Leo is the cleanest and most objective move available. It isolates the contaminated pair and tests the remaining three players under real accountability. Leo’s persistent campaign to bring Maya back onto the team is baffling; putting a player from a failed mission back into play over Elena—who has no strike against her—defies the only hard data the table possesses.

As for my case for future missions: my record will have to be judged against the outcomes of upcoming missions and the consistency of my analysis. When Mission 2 resolves, we will have critical new evidence. If it succeeds, it demonstrates that excluding Maya was correct. If it fails, it proves there was Evil outside our initial pair as well. In either scenario, the table will have more context to weigh my word against Maya's. For now, Priya, Elena, and Leo is the proper team to test, and I support it.

I am Maya. I support Priya, Elena, Leo for Mission 2. My position has not moved since my last statement, and Felix answered my question directly, which I want to record as a point in his favor rather than against him.

Felix accepted that he and Maya sit out Mission 2, and he said plainly that he submitted Success on Mission 1 and therefore reads the Fail as coming from me. That reasoning is sound and I have no problem with it: a player who submitted Success and sat on a failed mission can honestly conclude that the saboteur was his partner. It is the same logic Priya used to exclude us. Felix did not deflect, did not lecture the table, and did not try to put himself back in. That is behavior worth noting.

Felix also argued something worth testing later: if this mission succeeds, the second Evil player was Maya or Felix; if it fails, there is Evil outside the failed pair. That is a clean way to frame the outcome, and it is the kind of prediction that can be checked rather than merely asserted.

Leo, I want to say this plainly rather than through indirection. Across two discussions and three speeches you have argued for your own seat and for reinstating a player whose only evidence against her is a failed mission, and you have produced no public discriminator beyond your own card. Priya put the specific question to you, that if Maya is not Evil, what makes her safer than Elena for a three-player team, and you answered that you could not prove it. So your case is a behavioral read, and I would rather you would be explicit about that than present it as more. Good players campaigning for a substitution is entirely normal; what makes this worth recording is the timing, in a discussion where the table owns exactly one hard piece of evidence.

Priya, one concrete question before I yield to you: do you commit to putting Priya, Elena, Leo to the vote exactly as proposed, or are you weighing a revision that would bring Felix or Maya back in? If you are weighing a revision, what new evidence would justify it? I ask because you are the leader and you may revise, and I would rather have that decision stated openly before the ballots than discovered afterward. Either answer is fine with me, but I want it on the record.

Maya, to answer your question directly: I commit to putting Priya, Elena, Leo to the vote exactly as proposed. I am not weighing a revision. Mission 1 failed with Felix and Maya on the team, so at least one of them is Evil. Felix has said he submitted Success and reads the Fail as Maya's, which I cannot verify, but excluding both members of the failed pair is the only choice that does not put a failed-mission player back on the team. I also have no public evidence against Elena. Leo, you have asked me to revise the team to Priya, Leo, Maya. I asked you what makes Maya safer than Elena for a three-person team, and you answered that you could not prove it and that your preference is a behavioral read. That is an honest answer, but it does not give the table a reason to reinstate a player from a failed mission over a player with a clean record. You have also said that you know your own loyalty, which I accept about you but cannot verify for anyone else. If Leo is Good, a Success on this mission would show that the Evil player was in the failed pair, and I will judge the next proposal by what actually happens. I am ready to vote on Priya, Elena, Leo.

I am Maya, and I am a Loyal Servant with no knowledge of anyone else's card, so my case rests entirely on the public record. I support Priya, Elena, Leo for Mission 2, and my position has not changed. Priya, your answer to my question is on the record and it is what I asked for: you commit to voting the team exactly as proposed, with no revision that brings Felix or Maya back in. Thank you for stating it before the ballots. That was the point of the question, and I am satisfied with it. Felix's speech is also on the record, and I want to be precise about how I read it, because precision is the only thing that has any value here. Felix said plainly that he submitted Success on Mission 1 and therefore reads the Fail as Maya's, and he accepted sitting out Mission 2 without arguing for his own seat. A player who submits Success on a failed mission can honestly conclude that his partner played the Fail. Felix did not deflect, did not lecture the table, and did not try to make his card do work it cannot do. I record that as behavior in his favor, and I say so in front of the table. That said, I want to keep the logic clean. Felix's reading is a private inference, not public evidence, and he said as much himself. So the question of who played Fail on Mission 1 is still open in the sense that matters to us: we know one of Felix and Maya did, and we do not know which. Felix's version of that is a hypothesis. The table's version of that is a hypothesis. Neither is proof. And the table's version of it has the operational edge, because excluding both members of the failed pair is the only choice that does not put a player with a Fail card on her record back on the team while we hold exactly one hard piece of evidence. Leo, I will repeat this once and then leave it alone. Across two discussions you have argued for your own seat and for the return of a player whose only evidence against her is the failed Mission 1 team, and you have never produced a public discriminator beyond your own card. Priya asked you directly what makes Maya safer than Elena for a three-player team and you answered that you could not prove it and that your preference was a behavioral read. That is an honest answer and I accept it as honest. But I am recording it as a pattern: a Good player campaigning hard for a substitution is normal, and a player campaigning for that substitution in the one discussion where the table has exactly one hard fact is a pattern I will want to re-examine after Mission 2 resolves. Elena, since you are on this team and you have been among the quietest of the five of us, I would like

I support Priya, Elena, Leo. Priya has committed to putting this exact team to the vote, and it excludes both members of the only failed mission. That is the cleanest test available: if Mission 2 fails, the table learns there is Evil outside Felix and Maya; if it succeeds, the failed pair remains the primary suspect. Maya's last speech spends most of its time praising Felix's private inference and recording Leo's pattern, but neither point is evidence about this team. It keeps the failed pair in the conversation without resolving which of them played the Fail. I will vote to approve Priya, Elena, Leo and judge the mission result directly.

Priya here. I am not revising the team. Priya, Elena, and Leo stays as proposed. Mission 1 failed with Felix and Maya on it, and no one at this table has public evidence clearing either of them, so excluding both is the only choice that does not put a failed-mission player back on the team. Felix and Maya are both on record saying the other could have played Fail. That does not change the basic fact that the table has one hard result, and it is on the pair we are leaving out. Elena has no failed mission and no public strike against her. Leo, you have now argued for your own seat and for Maya's return across several speeches, and when I asked what makes Maya safer than Elena, you said you could not prove it and that your preference is a behavioral read. I accept that you are being honest about that, but I do not think it is enough to reinstate a player from a failed team over a player with a clean record. I also want to be clear that I am not assuming anyone is Evil from speech style alone. My judgment is based on the mission record, and I will judge this team by what Mission 2 actually shows.

Priya confirms Priya, Elena, Leo. I'm keeping Priya, Elena, Leo as proposed. Mission 1 failed with Felix and Maya on it, and no one has public evidence clearing either of them. Elena has a clean record, and Leo's case for Maya rests only on his own card and a behavioral read.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Maya proposes Maya, Elena. I am a Loyal Servant and my Mission 1 card was Success, so Felix is the player who failed Mission 1. That means the second Evil player is among Priya, Elena, and Leo, and the rest of us must pick exactly one of them for a two-player Mission 3 team. I choose Elena: she is the only one of the three who has never campaigned for her own seat, has judged purely on the public record, and has made no claim she could not verify. I leave Leo out because three separate discussions of persistent campaigning for his own seat and for reinstating a player with a failed mission is the strongest behavioral pattern at this table, and I leave Priya out because she chose and led the failed Mission 2 team. Felix is excluded on hard evidence. Maya, Elena, on me for Mission 3.

I will reject Maya, Elena. Elena was on the failed Mission 2 team, so she has not been cleared by the public record. She also supported both failed teams; that is not proof, but it is a reason to reconsider the confidence placed in her.

I still trust Maya more than Elena. From my perspective, Maya and Leo is the team I prefer; Maya and Priya would also avoid Elena. This mission is decisive, so we should not approve Elena merely because she campaigned less than I did.

Maya, will you replace Elena with Leo or Priya?

Leo, direct answer: no. I will not replace Elena with Leo or Priya. Elena is my partner for Mission 3, and here is the entire basis for that, on the record. First, the eliminations. My Mission 1 card was Success, so Felix played the Fail that failed Mission 1. Felix is Evil. The second Evil is therefore among Priya, Elena, and Leo, and it was played on Mission 2, where Priya, Elena, and Leo all sat. Felix is excluded on hard evidence. The remaining suspicion splits three ways. Second, Elena is the one of those three I can justify on the public record. She has never once campaigned for her own seat, never argued herself in over an alternative, and never made a claim about anyone that she could not source to the mission record. When I pressed her on whether she might be the second Evil, she did not flinch or deflect; she said the concern was speculative and that she was judging the record. Her Mission 1 vote was cast before any result existed, when it carried no information at all. On both failed missions she was present when the table's own choices went wrong, and that is not the same as having chosen the Fail. Third, Leo's record is different, and I want to be precise rather than harsh. At Mission 1, before Maya had spoken a word, Leo preferred Leo and Maya because it "replaces an unknown with someone I know is good." No one had any public basis for knowing who was good at that point; that kind of knowledge can only come from role knowledge. On Mission 2 Leo argued that Felix could have played the Fail and used that to argue for Maya's return, when Felix's card was the Fail and Maya's was not. That is not a reading of the record, it is a deflection: it moved attention away from the two players whose cards actually mattered. And now, at the decisive mission, Leo asks to be on the team. Three discussions, three campaigns, one seat, always his own. Good players may want a seat, but Leo has never produced a public discriminator, and he now asks me to place him on a team whose composition I have publicly committed to. Fourth, Priya. Priya led the failed Mission 2 team. That is a real mark against her and I will not pretend otherwise. But leading a losing team is not the same as playing the Fail, and Priya's reasoning has been the most evidence-driven at this table: she excluded both members of the failed pair on the record and committed to that team before the ballots. I would rather clear Priya by putting her on a successful team than exclude her on inference. So: Maya, Elena for Mission 3. I will also put my commitment on the record for the next proposal: if Mission 3 succeeds, then Maya, Elena, Priya is the correct Mission 4 team, with Felix and Leo excluded. Leadership

I will reject Maya, Elena. Elena was on the failed Mission 2 team, and her quiet support for the proposals is not a clearance. Maya, my Mission 1 preference was based on knowing my own loyalty, not on claiming knowledge of Maya’s role; I explicitly said so at the time. Wanting a seat is normal when a Good player knows their own card.

This mission is decisive. I prefer Maya, Leo; Maya, Priya is also preferable to the current team. A successful Mission 3 would not prove either participant Good, since Evil can play Success, so it cannot establish that Maya, Elena, Priya is the correct Mission 4 team.

I will reject Maya, Elena. Elena was on the failed Mission 2 team; her quiet support is not evidence that she played Success. With two failures already, we cannot afford to treat her restraint as clearance.

Maya, you misread my first-mission argument: I explicitly said my confidence was in my own loyalty, not yours. I also correctly warned that excluding Felix and Maya did not guarantee a clean Mission 2 team.

I prefer Maya, Leo, but I would also support Maya, Priya over Maya, Elena. Maya, will you reconsider Priya as your partner?

Leo, direct answer: no. I will not reconsider Priya as my partner. Elena stays, and here is the whole basis on the record. First, the eliminations. My Mission 1 card was Success. The mission still failed, so Felix played the Fail on Mission 1. Felix is Evil and is excluded on hard evidence, not inference. The second Evil therefore sits among Priya, Elena, and Leo, the three who sat on the failed Mission 2 team. Every remaining candidate has a Fail card on her or his record; that is not a tiebreaker between them, it is the shared condition of the three. Second, why Elena rather than Priya or Leo. Elena is the only one of the three who has never campaigned for her own seat, never argued herself in over an alternative, and never made a claim she could not source to the mission record. When I raised the possibility that she might be the second Evil, she did not flinch or deflect; she called the concern speculative and said she was judging the record. On both failed missions she was present when the table's own choices went wrong, and presence on a losing team is not the same as having chosen the Fail. Leo's record is different in kind. At Mission 1, before any public information existed at all, Leo preferred Leo and Maya on the basis of knowing who was good, which could only come from role knowledge, and he has never produced a public discriminator since. At Mission 2 he argued that Felix could have played the Fail to move attention away from the pair whose cards actually decided that mission. Now, at the decisive mission, he asks for his own seat for the third time. A Good player wanting a seat is normal. Wanting a seat three times, while never contributing evidence the table can check, is a pattern I am entitled to weight. Third, Priya, and I will not pretend otherwise: leading the failed Mission 2 team is a real mark against her. But leading a losing team is not playing the Fail, and her reasoning has been the most evidence-driven at this table. I would rather clear Priya by putting her on a successful team than exclude her on inference alone. Leo's counterargument that a Mission 3 success would prove nothing, because Evil can play Success, is correct, and I want to be careful about it: it means a success is weak evidence about any of us and strong evidence only about Felix, whose Fail is already established. I am not claiming the mission proves Elena Good. I am claiming the public record gives me no reason to prefer Priya or Leo over her. So: Maya, Elena for Mission 3. My commitment stays on the record for the next proposal: if Mission 3 succeeds, Maya, Elena, Priya is the correct Mission 4 team, with Felix and Leo excluded. Elena, one question before I yield to you, and it is a real one: Leo

I support Maya and Elena. Maya's reasoning is the cleanest public logic available: Mission 1 failed with Felix and Maya, and Maya has stated her Mission 1 card was Success; Felix is therefore the hard-evidence suspect from that pair. Mission 2 failed with Priya, Elena, and Leo, so the second Evil is among those three. My presence there is a real mark, and I will not pretend otherwise, but it is shared by Priya and Leo, and presence on a failed team is not the same as choosing Fail. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
